title: A Seek and Find Challenge for the First Weeks of School
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart introduces a first-weeks-of-school practice distinct from his usual name-memorization and routine-building work: deliberately seeking out something to like about each student he teaches. He frames the origin of the idea in a compliment from his daughter, who told him he's good at liking people, all kinds of people, which he traces to years of teaching practice at finding likeable qualities in anyone. He recasts the exercise as a spiritual discipline in his specific sense of the term, an intentional practice for strengthening one's will, rather than a soft, incidental habit, comparing it to a weightlifter's training. He shares several concrete, admittedly subjective examples from his own classroom to show that the observations don't need to be provable or shared interests, just genuinely felt. The payoff, he argues, comes later: banked observations of likeability become a resource a teacher can draw on to stay warm and resolved during the inevitable hard conversations with a struggling student.
points: Stuart frames "finding something to like about each student" as a spiritual discipline in his specific sense, an intentional will-strengthening practice, not a vague be-nice sentiment.
His examples deliberately stay subjective and unprovable (a hat, a resemblance, kind eyes) to make the point that the exercise doesn't require objective common ground with a student.

The strategic payoff is banked goodwill: recalling these liked qualities is what lets a teacher approach a later hard conversation with a struggling student from a place of liking and loving rather than fear or anger.
quotes: She said, Dad, you're really good at liking people, all kinds of people. Thank you so much, my love, I said. I guess my job as a teacher gives me lots of practice with this.
There are things to like about anyone, and finding these things is a profitable enterprise.

Finding something to like about each student, then, isn't so much a task for me as it is a way of working out and gaining strength. It is a way of developing my will, of building strength in my spirit.
As you can see, most of these are subjective. They're the ways students make me feel, the things I sense about them. For this exercise, that's great.

They don't need to be hard, objective facts. They don't need to be things you have in common with students. They don't need to be things you can prove. But they do need to exist. You do need to find them.
When you're looking out at those individual faces, watching them begin a warm-up or discuss in groups, you can think about all the things you like about these human beings.
These fond moments will be there, ready to stoke your resolve not from a place of fear or anger, but from a place of liking and loving.
